name: Bilal Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on ancillary gear at Red Flats, which is a big open-cut iron ore mine. Mostly I drive a water cart, spraying the haul roads so the dust doesn't choke everyone, and some days they put me on the grader to keep the roads smooth for the big trucks. It sounds boring but if the roads are bad, the whole mine slows down, so I take it seriously.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a shift at a supermarket distribution centre for nine years, forklifts and pickers. Then they put in an automated warehouse, the kind with little robots running on a grid, and my team went from forty people to eleven. I got a decent payout, used part of it to buy into some shares, and took a junior spot at the mine, which pays better anyway. My wife Marta teaches at the primary school and we've got Kuba, who's eleven, and Lena, who's eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm learning again; I'm still pretty rough on the grader, my blade work is wavy, but I'm getting there. I use AI on my phone every day: I ask it about haul road design, I had it explain the mine plan to me in plain words. What wears me out is the heat. Summer on a water cart is like sitting in an oven that's spraying a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit surprised, because I watched robots take my last job. I'd probably post something like, well, the hype train ran out of track. And I'd tell the guys on the crew not to get too comfortable, because the robots at my old warehouse weren't hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. I'd keep getting better on the grader and probably move up faster than most. A small part of me would be disappointed, because I like this stuff and I thought it would be exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the AI tools for what they're good at, like studying for my next ticket. I'd keep adding to the shares every month and pay a bit extra on the mortgage. I'd probably push the mine to try out some of the planning tools, because even small time savings would make my shifts easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of boredom mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your old warehouse. Does that experience change how you'd hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I know it's not all hype. I've already been replaced by a robot once, so I don't believe anyone who says it can't happen. Even in this picture, some of it is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Hemi, the supervisor on our crew. He's been there twenty years and he's very sceptical. We have this running joke where I tell him about some new tool and he says, can it make a decent coffee yet.

S0.say: He'd say he's surprised, because robots really did take his last job, and he'd warn his crew not to get too comfortable.
S0.think: He thinks he'd be fine and move up quickly, but would be slightly disappointed because he finds the technology exciting.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI to study for his next ticket, adds to his shares monthly, pays extra on the mortgage, and nudges the mine to try planning tools.
S0.quote: I've already been replaced by a robot once, so I don't believe anyone who says it can't happen.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is the rare person who sounds let down by AI fizzling out. His warehouse experience means he never treats automation as hype, even in this scenario. He already uses AI daily to learn his new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board early and make the company pay for the training. I'd tell people at work: I saw this at the warehouse, the ones who moved first got the new jobs. Online I'd say the companies saving millions should be funding the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my chance. Water carts and graders are already going driverless at some mines, so my job won't last, but somebody has to run the control room. I'd rather be watching ten machines than driving one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within the first month I'd ask about the remote operations centre and what tickets it needs. I'd use my evenings with AI tutorials to learn the fleet software. In the first year I'd apply for every training spot, and if the mine wouldn't pay, I'd pay for a course myself from savings. I'd also keep pushing the union to get a training deal for everyone, not just keen guys like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. But I'd feel guilty about it when I look at some of the older guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy, Darren, he's fifty-six and drives the grader beautifully. He can't use a smartphone properly. I'd be moving up into the control room while Darren is being shown the door, and that's not a good feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for a course yourself. How much would you put in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five or six thousand. We could do it without touching the mortgage. Marta would want to see the course outline first, and she'd be right.

S1.say: He'd tell people to get on board early and make the company pay for training. Online he'd argue that companies saving millions should fund the transition.
S1.think: He sees it as a chance to move into the remote operations centre. He'd rather watch ten machines than drive one.
S1.do: Asks about the remote operations centre in the first month, studies fleet software with AI tutorials in the evenings, pays up to six thousand for a course if needed, and pushes the union for training for all.
S1.feel: Calm, a little excited, and guilty about older colleagues.
S1.quote: I'd be moving up into the control room while Darren is being shown the door, and that's not a good feeling.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal treats steady disruption as an opportunity because he's been through it before. His progressive views show in wanting the training deal for everyone. The guilt he feels about his colleague Darren is the most emotional part of this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to tax the companies that own the robots and share it out. I'd post that loudly. I'd say it at the union meeting too, because the old deals won't cover this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my plan of moving into the control room doesn't work in this picture. If AI can do almost any job, it can watch the screens too. So for the first time I'd feel like being quick doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move more of our savings into shares in companies building the robots, because if they own the future, I want a slice. I'd keep working as long as they'd let me, and save every bonus. I'd join any campaign for a robot tax or a universal basic income, which means everyone gets a basic payment no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm used to being the guy who's ahead of the change, and here there's no ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years of warning compare with no warning at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough time to move money but not enough to move careers. I'd use the two years to get our finances right rather than chasing a course that'd be useless by the time I finished it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting savings into shares is a risk. What does Marta think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it. She'd say we need cash, not bets. We'd probably meet in the middle, half in shares and half in the bank, which is how we decide everything.

S2.say: He'd say governments must tax the companies that own the robots and share the gains. He'd raise it at union meetings because old deals won't cover this.
S2.think: He realises his plan of moving to the control room fails if AI can do almost any job. For once, being quick doesn't protect him.
S2.do: Moves part of the savings into shares in robot makers, works and saves every bonus as long as possible, and joins campaigns for a robot tax and a universal basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious and thrown, because there's no getting ahead of it.
S2.quote: We'd probably meet in the middle, half in shares and half in the bank, which is how we decide everything.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario that takes away Bilal's usual tool, which is moving first. His answer shifts from careers to money: owning a piece of the robots. His public politics and private investing fit together rather than contradict each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper safety net if we stop arguing and start now. I'd push the union and local politicians on a retraining fund and a robot tax. Online, I'd probably make a video about my warehouse story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a sweet spot for me. I could get two or three years in the control room before the AI takes that too, and earn well while I do. I'd use that time to build something on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd get into the remote operations centre. I'd keep buying shares in automation companies each month. By year two or three I'd start a side business, maybe helping small farms and businesses around town set up AI tools, since I already use them every day and most people round here don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help other people set up AI tools. Isn't that work AI could do too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. But people round here would rather have a guy they know from the footy club show them than talk to a chatbot. The robot can do the job, but it can't buy you a beer after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kuba already uses AI more than I do. I'd tell him the tools aren't the scary part, it's who owns them. And I'd tell Lena she can be whatever she wants, which is the same thing I'd say anyway.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to build a safety net if everyone starts now, and he'd push for a retraining fund and a robot tax, maybe telling his warehouse story online.
S3.think: He sees five years as a sweet spot: a few well-paid years in the control room, then a side business before AI takes that over too.
S3.do: Moves into the remote operations centre in year one, keeps buying automation shares monthly, and by year two or three starts a side business helping local farms and small firms set up AI tools.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: The robot can do the job, but it can't buy you a beer after.
S3.fieldNote: With a bit of time Bilal's confidence returns, and he builds a staircase of plans. He bets that local trust will outlast what AI can do. His message to his son, that ownership matters more than the tools, ties his politics to his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, and if we don't, it's a political failure, not a tech one. I'd get involved in the union's planning committee. I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well, I think. I'd be fifty-three, with the house nearly paid and a good few shares. My worry would be more for the town and the guys who don't move than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the control room job early and stay as long as it lasted. I'd study part-time for a technical diploma in automation and maintenance, because someone has to keep the robots running for a while. I'd grow the shares and the side business slowly, and set aside a fund for Kuba and Lena's studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy about the town, but calm for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does the decade change for you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm protecting money. With ten I'm building something. That's the difference. I'd have time to learn properly instead of grabbing whatever's closest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry about the town. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the shops on Ellis Street live on mine wages. If the mine runs with forty people instead of four hundred, the bakery and the tyre shop feel it first. I'd want the council planning for that now, not in year nine.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to get it right and failing would be a political failure. He'd join the union's planning committee and post about it often.
S4.think: He thinks he'd do well, being fifty-three with a nearly paid house and shares. His worry is for the town and for colleagues who don't adapt.
S4.do: Takes a control room job early, studies part-time for a technical diploma in automation and maintenance, grows the shares and side business slowly, and sets up a study fund for his two children.
S4.feel: Mostly calm for his family, uneasy for the town.
S4.quote: With two years I'm protecting money. With ten I'm building something.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Bilal moves from protecting to building. His concern shifts outward to the town's shops on Ellis Street, which fits his progressive view. He's the clearest example of someone whose adaptability and savings combine to keep him steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where moving fast doesn't help. What would help is a tax on robot-run companies paid into a fund that gives people a basic income and free retraining, set up before it hits, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people if it's happened to them before. It changes how you see it. When the warehouse went robotic, the robots weren't the cruel part. The cruel part was the meeting where they read out forty names.

headlineQuote: When the warehouse went robotic, the robots weren't the cruel part. The cruel part was the meeting where they read out forty names.
portrait: Bilal Kowalski is a 43-year-old water cart and grader driver at an open-cut iron ore mine, still rough on the grader blade but learning fast. He was replaced by robots once already at a warehouse, used the payout to buy shares and moved into mining. He's married to a primary teacher, has two kids, uses AI every day and wants companies taxed to fund retraining and a basic income. He's calm through the slower scenarios, eyeing the remote control room, and only anxious with two-year AGI, where being quick no longer protects him.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it's the only one where moving fast doesn't help.
whatWouldHelp: A tax on robot-run companies paying into a fund for a basic income and free retraining, set up before the change hits.
